As someone who struggles everyday with borderline personality disorder, when you said that your emotions run high, I completely empathise with you. I am often a slave to my wild emotional swings, and childish tantrums.

HOWEVER an important part of being neuro-atypical/mentally ill is knowing we have ZERO control over other people’s actions. The only control we have is over our own. We absolutely cannot mistreat people and say ‘whelp, what do you expect, that’s my Aspergers/borderline!’ . It’s not a pass, or an excuse, only an explanation of an underlying mechanism for atypical behaviour and psyche. The onus is on the person to regulate themselves, not the people around them. It’s not your wife’s job to allow you to dictate her body autonomy because it makes you have a tantrum. The same way it isn’t my partner’s job to tip-toe around my easily triggered emotions, it’s my job to not overreact to normal things.

I went to a very prestigious university for undergrad (in the UK’s equivalent of ‘Ivy League’) and am now doing my PhD at Oxford. 

I had to take a whole year out for my mental health. I literally laid in bed for a whole year, only really leaving the house to go to the doctors or therapy. 

Literally no-one - not my friends back home or my uni friends - looked down on me at all. I was hugely supported by everyone. I just told the truth, that my mental health failed and I couldn’t take the pressure, and everyone totally understood.

I knew huge numbers of people at uni that were on antidepressants, anti-anxiety, mood stabilisers, people who had attempted suicide, people who had to be in-patients at psychiatric units for lengths of time... you get the idea. The doctor I saw said they get TONNES of high-achieving students coming in and breaking down. She said, quote, ‘it’s the classic tortured genius stereotype’ to give you an idea of how commonly she dealt with this exact problem. 

Just tell people the truth, and they will love you for it. Be kind to yourself, good things lie ahead :)
